PART 1: NARRATION READY
What you're looking at with REND1 is a transformer that is working significantly harder than it has to — and paying a real cost for that every single month. The power factor for June averaged 79.8 percent. That means roughly one dollar in every five that your utility is delivering to this transformer is not doing useful work. It is circulating as reactive current — heating conductors, loading the transformer core, and expanding the apparent power demand without moving a single process forward. The monthly price tag on that inefficiency is approximately $33,460 in wasted energy costs for June alone. Annualized, that is roughly $662,000 per year — running out the door in an untuned field. The reactive load is the engine of that waste. The average reactive draw was 698.6 kVAR across the month. The peak hit 1,132.9 kVAR — nearly as large as the real power demand of 1,295 kilowatts. That is a structural imbalance in the field, not a temporary spike. The thermal consequence is 885,600 BTU per hour of waste heat. That heat burden is loading your cooling systems — about $25.60 per hour and 129.8 kilowatts of cooling overhead tied directly to electrical inefficiency on this one transformer. And the voltage picture adds urgency. The operating band runs consistently below the 480-volt nominal. A severe sag to 357.5 volts was recorded early in the month — more than 120 volts below nominal. On a food processing and cold storage operation, that kind of sag event stresses motor drives, risks VFD fault trips, and threatens process continuity. The correction path is clear: three H490 units, delivering 1,200 kVAR of reactive compensation. Projected power factor correction to 99.5 percent. Planning investment approximately $500,000 to $650,000 installed — with substantial recovery of that annual waste rate driving the payback. This field is drifting in the wrong direction every month it goes untuned. ---

PART 2: EXECUTIVE SHORT
REND1 is an untuned field carrying a serious reactive burden — and the numbers are hard to ignore. Power factor at 79.8 percent. Reactive peak at 1,132.9 kVAR. Monthly waste roughly $33,460 — about $662,000 per year annualized. Thermal burden near 885,600 BTU per hour, generating approximately $25.60 per hour in cooling overhead. The voltage field is under stress too. A severe sag to 357.5 volts was recorded in June — more than 120 volts below the 480-volt nominal — with consistent sub-nominal dips throughout the month. For a food processing operation, that is a device health risk you cannot ignore. The correction requires three H490 units — 1,200 kVAR total capacity — to bring the field to 99.5 percent power factor. Planning investment estimate is roughly $500,000 to about $650,000 installed. The annual waste this field is currently generating makes that investment conversation worth having now, because this field does not improve on its own. Without correction, heat burden grows, insulation ages faster, and the waste cost compounds month over month. --- Pricing note: these figures are planning-level estimates, not final quotes. Final installed pricing depends on engineering scope, labor, and site conditions. For planning, estimated installed investment is roughly $28,400 to $38,500.

PART 3: ENGINEERING DETAILED
Let me walk you through the complete picture on REND1 — because this field tells a detailed and important story. We are looking at a full June dataset — 43,200 minutes of measurement across this transformer's operation at the Livingston facility. The field mode is untuned, meaning no reactive compensation is currently in place. And you can see the consequences of that across every view we have. Start with the power factor. The June average was 79.8 percent. The theoretical maximum is 100 percent — meaning every volt-amp delivered to the transformer becomes productive kilowatts of real work. At 79.8 percent, you are achieving that on less than four out of every five volt-amps delivered. The remaining fraction — and it is a meaningful fraction — is reactive current. It circulates. It heats things. It expands the apparent power demand. And your utility charges you for it. The reactive load in numbers: 698.6 kVAR average, peaking at 1,132.9 kVAR maximum. To frame that peak — your real power peak demand was 1,295.2 kilowatts. So at the reactive peak, you were carrying reactive current nearly equal in magnitude to your entire real production load. The transformer was, in effect, serving two full-size loads at once — one doing work, one just circulating heat. The current burden that creates is substantial. The M view confirms a peak amperage of 1,693.3 amps. Every amp above what the real load actually requires is traveling through every conductor, every connection, and every winding in the circuit — adding heat at every step. That heat accumulates into a thermal burden of approximately 885,600 BTU per hour. I want you to picture what that means concretely. It is equivalent to roughly 74 tons of air conditioning demand — generated purely by electrical inefficiency on this one transformer. And your facility's cooling systems are absorbing that burden, to the tune of about $25.60 per hour and 129.8 kilowatts of cooling load. That cooling cost is a direct subsidy from your mechanical systems to your electrical inefficiency. The total waste cost for June was approximately $33,460. Annualized, that projects to roughly $662,000 per year. That is the economic baseline for the correction conversation. Now the voltage field adds a different dimension of urgency. The month averaged 476.6 volts — already below the 480-volt nominal. But within that average, we see seven annotated drop events, most landing in the 454 to 461 volt range. For motor-driven loads and variable frequency drives on a 480-volt bus, operating 19 to 25 volts below nominal on a recurring basis creates elevated winding stress and increases the probability of nuisance trips during production. The event that stands out most is the sag to 357.5 volts recorded near the start of June. That is a drop of over 120 volts below nominal — approximately 25 percent under the design voltage of the system. At that level, drives can trip offline, motor starters can fail to pick up, and in a food processing environment, process temperature control can be interrupted. This is not a tolerable operating condition, and its root cause needs to be investigated — whether it is a large motor starting without soft-start protection, a switching event on the distribution bus, or an upstream fault. The harmonic environment is moderate — 5.8 percent iTHD average, 11.1 percent maximum. Not critical on its own, but worth factoring into the MPTS engineering scope. When you add reactive compensation capacitors to a field with meaningful harmonic content, you want to confirm there is no resonance interaction. Detuned reactor filters on the H490 array are the standard answer, and they should be evaluated for this site. The correction sizing is straightforward. Take the kVAR maximum of 1,132.9 kVAR, divide by 400, and round up. That gives you 2.83 — which rounds to three H490 units. Three units deliver 1,200 kVAR of correction capacity, sufficient to handle the peak reactive demand this field recorded in June. At a planning-level estimate of roughly $200,000 per H490 unit installed, the three-unit array represents a planning investment range of approximately $500,000 to about $650,000 — final scope depends on engineering review and site conditions. The projected outcome is a power factor correction to 99.5 percent. At that level, the reactive burden essentially disappears. The transformer stops heating itself with circulating current. The thermal load on your cooling systems drops substantially. And the approximately $662,000 per year in waste cost becomes substantially recoverable — with the majority of that recovery

REND1.field_condition_summary:
**REND1 — Untuned Field Condition Summary | Foster Farms Livingston HQ | June 2026**

The REND1 transformer is operating in a measurably stressed, untuned state. Every major indicator — power factor, reactive load, thermal burden, voltage stability, and cooling overhead — points to a field that is working significantly harder than it needs to, and delivering less usable power per ampere than it should.

The average power factor for the month sat at 79.8 percent. In practical terms, that means roughly one dollar in five that your utility delivers to this transformer is not doing productive work. It is circulating — heating windings, loading the transformer core, and expanding the current burden on every conductor in the circuit. The peak demand reached 1,295.2 kilowatts against a supply target of 1,380 kVA, which means this transformer is regularly approaching and breaching its effective operating ceiling during production hours.

The reactive load is the core problem here. The average reactive draw was 698.6 kVAR, and it spiked to a maximum of 1,132.9 kVAR — a reactive peak that is nearly as large as the entire real power demand. That is not a minor inefficiency. That is structural waste built into the daily operating rhythm of this facility.

The cost consequence is direct and significant. The BT view reports approximately $33,460 in wasted energy costs for this single dataset period, projecting to roughly $662,345 per year if this field runs uncorrected. The thermal burden associated with that reactive load is approximately 885,600 BTU per hour — a heat-generation rate that is feeding directly into the facility's cooling demand.

Without tuning assignment, this field will continue drifting. Reactive load tends to grow as motor insulation ages, as additional loads are added, and as the field's own heat burden accelerates degradation. The correction window is open now — the longer it remains untuned, the steeper the cumulative waste trajectory becomes.

REND1.voltage_stability_findings:
**REND1 — Voltage Stability Findings | June 2026**

The voltage picture for REND1 is one of the more concerning field health profiles in this review. The month-average voltage of 476.6 volts is already below the 480-volt nominal line — meaning on average, across all 43,200 minutes of June, this transformer was delivering slightly under-nominal voltage to the load. That alone is a yellow flag. But the detail within that average tells a harder story.

Across the voltage chart, at least seven distinct triangular drop events are annotated with specific voltage callout values. The majority of these dips land in the 454–461 volt range — consistently 19 to 25 volts below nominal. For motor drive systems, VFDs, and control electronics running on a 480-volt bus, that operating band creates elevated thermal stress on motor windings and increases the risk of nuisance VFD fault trips during production shifts.

The single most alarming data point in this view is the annotated sag to 357.5 volts, observed in the early June timeframe near the 260604 zone. A drop of over 120 volts below nominal is not a flicker — it is a severe sag event. At 357.5 volts on a 480-volt system, sensitive equipment is operating approximately 25 percent under nominal voltage. That level of sag can trip drives offline, stress motor starters, and in some cases cause momentary loss of process control on refrigeration or rendering systems.

And then there is the absolute minimum recorded voltage of 9.5 volts — a near-total collapse. This was not a brief transient. It is confirmed as a true electrical collapse event, likely coinciding with a planned site shutdown, but its presence in the dataset confirms that this field has experienced at least one complete power-off condition during the month.

Device health risk level for REND1 based on this voltage profile: **high**. A food processing and cold storage environment running compressors, rendering equipment, and HVAC loads cannot afford the kind of repeated sub-nominal sag this field is producing. Insulation life shortens, motor bearings stress under voltage imbalance, and control systems accumulate fault history that shortens their operational lifespan. This voltage profile deserves immediate engineering attention alongside the reactive correction work.

REND1.reactive_harmonic_findings:
**REND1 — Reactive and Harmonic Findings | June 2026**

The reactive stress signature on REND1 is both persistent and severe. The M view confirms what the BT header reports: this field carries a sustained reactive burden throughout every production hour, and it peaks at levels that demand correction.

The kVAR average across the month was 698.6 kVAR. That figure alone represents a substantial circulating reactive current that is occupying transformer capacity, generating heat, and increasing the apparent power demand without contributing a single watt of productive work. But averages can be misleading. The kVAR maximum recorded was 1,132.9 kVAR — at that peak, the reactive demand was approaching the level of the transformer's entire real power draw of 1,295.2 kilowatts. That kind of reactive-to-real ratio is the textbook definition of an inefficient, untuned power field.

The M view's red current trace confirms the current burden this creates. The peak amperage annotated in the chart reached 1,693.3 amps. That is a heavy current load, and that current is flowing through every conductor, connection, and winding in the circuit — heating everything it touches.

On the harmonic side, the iTHD average sits at 5.8 percent with a maximum of 11.1 percent. This is a moderate harmonic environment — not catastrophic as a standalone figure, but not benign either. In combination with the reactive stress and the elevated current burden, the harmonic content adds incremental heat to the transformer core and increases losses in motor windings. At 11.1 percent peak THD, any harmonic-sensitive equipment on this bus — including variable frequency drives and precision temperature controls — is operating in a noisier electrical environment than optimal. The harmonic contribution also complicates power factor correction planning slightly, since uncorrected harmonics can interact with capacitor banks if not properly filtered.

Together, the reactive and harmonic profile of REND1 presents a clear picture: this is a transformer carrying significantly more apparent power than it needs to, running hotter than it should, and delivering a noisier field to its loads than the equipment is designed to tolerate long-term.

REND1.operational_stress_interpretation:
**REND1 — Operational Stress Interpretation | June 2026**

The operational picture assembled from the BT and M views reveals a transformer working at — and frequently beyond — its effective demand ceiling across a full month of production. This is not a facility with spare transformer capacity sitting idle. REND1 is being pushed hard, and the waste embedded in that push is measurable and costly.

During active production blocks, the supplied kVA consistently rides at or above the 1,380 kVA daily target line. Visual assessment of the BT chart suggests approximately 60 to 70 percent of active production hours are running at or above that ceiling — meaning the transformer is regularly operating in the zone where reactive loading begins to create measurable thermal stress rather than just efficiency loss. When you hold a transformer near or above its demand ceiling for sustained periods with a 79.8 percent power factor, you are not just wasting money on reactive charges — you are accelerating the thermal aging of the transformer's insulation system.

The thermal burden quantifies that stress directly: approximately 885,600 BTU per hour. To put that in perspective, that is the heat equivalent of roughly 74 tons of air conditioning demand generated purely by electrical waste. And that heat has to go somewhere — into the transformer enclosure, into the surrounding air, and into your facility cooling system. The reported cooling cost of approximately $25.60 per hour and 129.8 kilowatts confirms that a meaningful portion of your facility's cooling overhead is directly subsidizing electrical inefficiency on this one transformer.

The three distinct low/zero-production windows detected in the BT view — estimated at approximately 4 to 6 cumulative days across June — likely represent planned weekend or holiday shutdowns. These are normal for food processing operations. But the electrical collapse event confirmed by the 9.5-volt minimum in the voltage view adds an unplanned dimension to that downtime picture. At least once in June, REND1's field experienced a full voltage collapse — an event that, in a food processing cold storage environment, carries real risk of product temperature excursion and refrigeration recovery time.

The untuned nature of this field means every one of these stress indicators is compounding month over month. Without correction, reactive load tends to grow as motor fleets age, thermal stress continues to shorten insulation life, and the cost curve trends upward rather than flat.

REND1.simulated_mpts_outcome:
**REND1 — Simulated MPTS Outcome | June 2026**

The MPTS correction scenario for REND1 begins with the sizing calculation. The kVAR MAX from the BT header is 1,132.9 kVAR. Applying the standard sizing rule — kVAR MAX divided by 400, rounded up — yields 1,132.9 ÷ 400 = 2.83, which rounds up to **3 H490 units**. That is a three-unit correction array, delivering up to 1,200 kVAR of reactive compensation capacity — sufficient to address the peak reactive demand recorded in June.

At a planning-level installed estimate of approximately $200,000 per H490 unit, a three-unit array represents a planning investment range of roughly $500,000 to $650,000 installed — final scope and site conditions will determine actual engineering costs, and this range is for planning purposes only, not a binding quote.

The projected outcome, based on the S-view simulation data, is a power factor correction to 99.5 percent. At that corrected power factor, the reactive current that is currently consuming transformer capacity, generating heat, and inflating apparent power demand is substantially neutralized. The kVAR burden — currently averaging 698.6 kVAR and peaking at 1,132.9 kVAR — drops to a small residual fraction. The transformer effectively gains back capacity it has been spending on reactive circulation, which means the same real work output now requires meaningfully less apparent power draw.

The annual waste currently running at approximately $662,345 per year represents the economic target for recovery. MPTS correction does not recover 100 percent of that figure — some residual losses remain — but the substantial majority of the reactive waste component is recoverable. At the estimated waste rate and a three-unit investment, the payback horizon depends on final recovered savings, which the S-view will quantify precisely once available. As a planning reference, significant reactive waste recoveries at this scale typically produce payback periods in the range of 12 to 36 months under full production conditions.

Beyond the economics, the thermal burden reduction is equally important for this facility. Dropping from 885,600 BTU per hour of electrical waste heat toward a much lower corrected-state figure directly reduces the load on facility cooling systems — potentially recovering a meaningful portion of the 129.8 kilowatts and approximately $25.60 per hour currently spent on cooling overhead tied to electrical waste. In a food processing environment where temperature control is operationally critical, that thermal relief has value well beyond the line-item cost savings.

REND1.recommended_engineering_attention_areas:
**REND1 — Recommended Engineering Attention Areas | June 2026**

**1. Reactive Compensation — Three-Unit H490 Array**
The 1,132.9 kVAR maximum reactive demand requires a three-H490-unit correction array at the REND1 service point. This is the primary intervention and should be scoped first. Engineering review should confirm bus configuration, capacitor placement, and harmonic filter compatibility given the 11.1 percent peak iTHD environment.

**2. Voltage Sag Investigation — 357.5V Event**
The severe sag to 357.5 volts near the 260604 zone requires a root-cause engineering review. This is not a normal operating transient. Potential causes include a large motor starting event without soft-start protection, a momentary upstream fault, or a switching event on the distribution bus. Until the cause is identified and mitigated, this type of sag event represents an ongoing risk to VFD equipment, motor windings, and process control continuity on the REND1 bus.

**3. Voltage Regulation and Sub-Nominal Operating Band**
The consistent operating band of approximately 454 to 461 volts — running 19 to 25 volts below the 480-volt nominal — warrants investigation of tap changer settings on the REND1 transformer. A tap adjustment or voltage regulator installation may be appropriate to bring the operating band closer to nominal and reduce motor winding stress across the facility's load fleet.

**4. Harmonic Environment Assessment**
With peak iTHD at 11.1 percent, a brief harmonic survey should accompany the MPTS engineering scope to confirm that capacitor bank placement does not inadvertently amplify any existing harmonic resonance conditions on the bus. Detuned reactor filters on the H490 array are worth evaluating for this site.

**5. Electrical Collapse Event Documentation**
The 9.5-volt minimum confirmed in the V view should be cross-referenced against facility operations logs for June to identify the specific event, confirm whether it was a planned shutdown or a fault-driven collapse, and assess whether any downstream equipment experienced damage, nuisance trips, or food safety temperature excursions during recovery.

**6. Transformer Thermal Life Assessment**
Given the sustained 885,600 BTU/hr thermal burden running through June and the likelihood that this profile has been ongoing for multiple prior months in an untuned state, a transformer thermal life assessment is warranted to evaluate insulation condition and establish a baseline for post-correction improvement tracking.
